item.content:encoded:
First off, I 100% agree with all of this. If there was a canon or hub for all of the Bright family stuff, I didn't know about it, and none of the individual articles/tales crosslink in any useful way. I have no way of finding this stuff without using the search tool1 or stumbling across it by accident.

The article doesn't stand on its own two feet, but it also doesn't direct me to a larger narrative in any way at all. A great example of an SCP that can both contribute to a canon while standing on its own would be SCP-4514. The article has some really weird stuff going on that hints at a greater narrative, and it ultimately pushes the reader towards the End of Death Hub, where they now have a bunch of SCPs and tales to continue the story with.

Also, you'll learn about Dr. Bright when you get to SCP-963. It's actually a great article, and it is pretty much solely responsible for all of the Dr. Bright stuff on this wiki. He has an amazing gimmick that allows us to make some really unique tales.

Footnotes
1. Which is next to useless on this site considering there are literally only 4 filter options (general keyword, page/forum, title keyword, author keyword).

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
Sorry, but this is just awful.

+ show block
– hide block

590 is one of the Bright family, and some of the bad things have been done to him to protect him from even worse things.
That would have made this a very good SCP. However, none of that information is in the SCP1. No, it's not implied, either. There is nothing in this SCP that suggests any links to this backstory of a sister that had an anomalous heritage that congenitally went or wrong or something (I'm talking about DrNietzche's explanation about SCP-321 and SCP-963). And when you view it without that extra backstory, it is yet another human with an unfortunate anomaly. Damaging him mentally to keep him compliant is actually clever, and could be seen as compassionate as well as practical. The rest don't hold up. Why the diet? Why do we need a guard to stop him from self-harm if he behaves like a regular 3 year old? What is with the "compassion is prohibited, see that you don't use a name other than 590" bit? Honestly, that just sounds like a bad ripoff of 231's personnel requirements. But OK, that part is meant for Dr Bright.

Who the hell is Dr Bright, and do you have any idea how much I don't care?
I have been on this website for months, I have read all of SCPs 001 through 591, plus some others. I know there is a Dr Bright, but that's it. I know a little about Clef's personality and antics, but not Bright's. I had absolutely no idea that there was a whole family, and I had no idea the Foundation was governed in large part by this dysfunctional supernatural family (I'm talking about what's going on in the tale that SCP-590 links to.).

I'm probably sounding pretty dumb, and I must have gotten a lot of stuff wrong, but again, I've read more than 600 SCPs and a bunch of tales. If I am so clueless, maybe SCP-590 is written very obtusely. Maybe it was meant as a layered thing: It's a regular SCP if you are not very familiar with Bright, it's a whole other tale if you are familiar. But as a regular SCP, it fails. I want to point out, in the discussion page, no one who didn't get the Bright family angle liked the SCP.

—-

If you applied that test, "would this work if it was the first SCP someone read?" It fails. It didn't work as the 600th SCP I read because I didn't even notice the backstory.

If you remember that SCPs are supposed to stand on their own legs and not depend on other SCPs to explain themselves, yeah it fails. It seems to require a whole body of SCP lore to appreciate.


As a courtesy to our readers on mobile devices, please collapse long posts. ~Zyn

If you think it's OK for an SCP to require 1 or 2 linked pages to be fully understood, this still fails! The only linked article is a tale (Code Brown) that makes things worse. Code Brown does one thing well: It lets us know 590 is not some random person, and there is a reason for why some of the things were done to him. However, this is really throwing a reader in the deep end, with all these weird characters grouped into the "Foundation side of the table" (What is the other side?), all the complicated relations and histories… Honestly, it is like the ending of a complicated book series. Worse, when SCP-590 is mentioned, he either shows some unexpected adult thinking and behavior, or is implied to have perceived Nobody just fine. Both of those things clash with the SCP-590 article itself.

On what level does it work?

Footnotes
1. Except for the linked tale, but I'll mention it later.

item.content:encoded:
So, the comments cleared the "mental retardation" bit for me but I still have some… issues with this. I'll put aside the question whether this is unnecessary cruelty or not. I have a minor but nagging problem with:

He is a tool to be used

I'd write:

It is a tool to be used

Just as I'd change all the respective "he"s to "it"s.
I had an impression that the Foundation purposely refers to all SCPs, including humanoid ones as "it" so I would expect this to be used especially in the case of SCP that has a note highlighting its "toolness".

Now, what about that gruel thing? As it is written now, it really seems like not only unnecessary cruelty but also… misplaced effort? I mean, they create it especially for this SCP. Why? Does it need a very specific diet? Or is it just to dehumanize it further, in the eyes of the staff? I feel like we're lacking some proper justification. Usually (in those skips I've managed to read so far) containment procedures are either explained or pretty much self-explanatory. Here, we can only guess blindly. And as much as I can see the value of not stating everything explicitly (even though, being a newbie, I usually miss most of the hidden references) but this feeding procedure seems like "let's make the kid's life as miserable as possbile" kind of thing rather than actual, sensible containment procedure.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
Seems pointlessly cruel, in the sense that… okay so the foundation is using this kid in a way that is absolutely torture, but we get very little detail to characterize that choice, and so it's kind of just a horrible thing for the sake of being horrible. Like do they use him in cases of absolute need, making this a "necessary" evil? Or do they let any researcher who loses a finger use him?

I think the reference to scp-500 hurts this too 'cause if both exist contemporary with one another, why would you ever use 500 on anyone but the kid? Just give him a boatload of diseases from different people and then heal him directly. Having him used inefficiently adds to my feeling that this is just horrible for no reason but itself.

The "mental retardation" bit is just awkward. I really dislike it, probably more than anything else in the skip. I think it's that there's a total lack of exploration of how spontaneous manifestation of three unnamed mental illnesses in a mentally typical individual would even present feels almost… offensive in a weird way.

Lastly, and this is maybe my biggest character beef with this article: Who the hell would use him? The Foundation is cold, not the people, so what kind of person is willing to personally press that button and break, essentially, a child's arm to fix their own? The article tells us this is something normal enough that you can submit a request for it, so I mean, who consciously makes that decision? This is why we need to know things like when and why they use him, and I mean, you could even say he heals you from the mental trauma of using him with the act of using him, and that would make sense of a lot of things, but there's just nothing.

Anyway, I'm down for this concept, but I like nothing about how it is presented here.

Edit: I figured out what really bothers me to the point of offense about this thing. The idea that Bright's actions are an act of mercy suggests to me that it's written from the perspective that the mentally disabled are less (or even un-) able to feel pain, loneliness, despair, or other emotions that torture and the total betrayal of one's humanity might spark. We've seen this attitude before in real world history. And the sad thing is, I could totally see that working in this article's favour, if it were being utilized as part of the horror; that some anachronistic scientist genuinely felt this made him less human. But it's not, and so I'm left feeling like we're meant to take for granted that Bright's actions are rational, acceptable acts of mercy.

item.content:encoded:
Consider this: SCP-500 is a panacea, but it's restricted to Level 4 access. The reason is obvious - we've only got 50 of the things, and we can't have every Researcher Joe popping a pill to cure his hangover. While there's no indication that 590 doesn't heal from maladies he absorbs (if they can be healed), due to the cumulative effect of injuries and the utility of his power he's off-limits. A paper cut won't kill you, but the scar tissue of a thousand papercuts might.

Also, consider the point of 590 - humanoid SCPs are not people, they are SCPs. 590 is a tool, not a person, and will be used as such. While this is the policy, human personnel don't always follow it. There are undoubtedly many who think 590 should be euthanized, and given its nature it would be incredibly easy to pull off - inject yourself with a deadly virus, or pour some dimethymercury on your skin, anything that's time-delayed, and then get 590 to heal your "flu." Easy access would logically be restricted as a result.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
The kindest thing that could've possibly been done was to such a tortured soul, having failed to truly save his little sister, was to be able to forget and *if he should remember one day, he be in such a mental state that he does not fully understand life or death. He gave himself to save an innocent, and for that he was rewarded with Ignorance. Ignorance of the pain of losing a sibling, the pain of watching a father slip into nihilistic despair, the constant doubts(Was this my fault?… and nightmares a mother must feel about her bundle of joy.

And then of course, there's the guilt from mother and father. I can hear, in my head, an older man sobbing quietly to himself, likely with a few glasses of whiskey to keep him company in a cold room, reading the files over and over and over again, muttering about how selfish it was of him to ask what he did of his son, knowing that he would've never said no. His little boy, so brave. Brave enough to risk everything just to have a baby sister.

Time passes, as it tends to do, and on the day the father knew his end was approaching, at his bedside was only one of his family. The mother had tied, his little boy was being kept somewhere so he might live some measure of life without having to deal with the soul-crushing burden he never deserved to bare. He motioned to his son to get closer, his voice raspy and breathing strained.

"Because of what we-….what I did, I know I was never much of a father to you after what happened. I can never make it up to you. Or your brother, your sister, mother. I just..-coughs-..I'm asking you this not as your father, but as one man to another. Please, promise me you'll keep them safe, to care for them like I was never able too, to make whatever is left of their lives as pleasant as you can."

After his father passed, that left only a doctor, his baby sister, and a brother. For his brother, he would take no chances. As hard as it was, he made it so that even if the memories manage to come back to him, life and death will be concepts his limited mental capacity to grasp. As for his sister, there was little more he could do other than what was already in place. But still, once a year, on a very special day, he makes a very special trip. It may say that he's merely doing first-hand documentation on SCP-321. To note any changes or new abnormalities. But while no one speaks it, his overseers and his underlings know.

Sometimes, on these very special days, he no longer loathes the amulet hanging from his neck. He may never die, but that also means he'll keep fulfilling that promise. Sometimes that's enough.

…whew, was not expecting that to come out long, but the writing spider bit me and I had to get it out. -crosses fingers- This all just head-canon obviously, and I'm one of those who thinks amnesiacs, while certainly useful and potent, aren't 100% effective.
